source: Rissanen (1978) Modeling by shortest data description
finding: Founding two-part MDL paper. The best model gives the shortest code for model plus data. Parameter cost is about (k/2) log n bits, which matches BIC.
numbers: Cited in Grunwald and Roos; not opened this session. Cost (k/2) log2 n bits for k parameters and n points.
limits: Paywalled. Two-part codes are only one MDL code; later work moved to NML and prequential codes.
agent_relevance: Gives a selection score: fit cost plus description cost. Fits our need for a simplicity price in selection.

source: Shtarkov (1987) Universal sequential coding of single messages
finding: Defines the normalised maximum likelihood (NML) code: best-fit probability of the data divided by the sum of best-fit probabilities over all possible data. It is the minimax-regret code.
numbers: Cited in Grunwald and Roos; not opened. Regret equals the log of the normaliser for every data sequence.
limits: Normaliser is infinite for many models with unbounded outcomes.
agent_relevance: NML has no prior. It is the clearest case where a code length is not a Bayes posterior under any prior.

source: Grunwald and Roos (2019) Minimum Description Length Revisited
finding: Every code length matches a probability, so MDL is not opposed to Bayes. But NML, two-part, Bayes and prequential codes are different universal distributions, and Bayes is only one choice. MDL replaces priors with luckiness functions v, and average-case with worst-case regret.
numbers: Eq 3: NML = max-likelihood of data over integral of max-likelihood over all data. Eq 5: v-MDL estimator = Bayes MAP when v is a density. Bernoulli NML complexity is within a constant of (1/2) log n; the constant uses the Jeffreys-prior integral.
quote: MDL can be seen as a powerful extension of both penalized likelihood and Bayesian approaches
limits: With v=1 the normaliser diverges for most unbounded models (e.g. normal location), so complexity is infinite. The fix is a non-uniform luckiness v, which is prior-like.
agent_relevance: Selection with priors: score hypotheses by -log p(data|h) minus log v(h), where v need not sum to one.

source: Grunwald and Roos (2019) NML versus Bayes
finding: NML equals a Bayes marginal only in special cases. For the Bernoulli model NML is close to Bayes with Jeffreys prior, but not equal. An exact NML-Bayes match for Gaussian regression holds only for a particular luckiness function; Bartlett et al 2013 show such matches are rare.
numbers: NML and Jeffreys-Bayes agree up to a vanishing term at large n for regular models; exact equality only in special cases (their Appendix A).
limits: This is the subfield claim. For fixed n NML is not horizon-independent; Bayes is.
agent_relevance: A worst-case code length cannot always be read as a posterior. Keep prior-based and worst-case scores separate.

source: Grunwald and Roos (2019) horizon problem
finding: NML needs the sample size n in advance. Bayes mixtures and prequential plug-in codes do not. Horizon-free codes close to NML were built to fix this.
numbers: Section 3.2: Bayesian universal codes solve the horizon issue but lack the NML worst-case regret meaning. Horizon-independent non-Bayesian codes are rare.
limits: Review text; no experiments here.
agent_relevance: Our agent has an unknown number of attempts. Sequential (prequential) scoring avoids fixing a budget in advance.

source: Grunwald and Roos (2019) minimax regret
finding: The minimax problem (best code against the worst data) has a solution only if the NML complexity is finite; then the unique solution is NML. This gives a guarantee without assuming the model is true.
numbers: Complexity = log of the integral of max-likelihood over all data; must be finite.
limits: The guarantee is relative to the best member of the model, not to truth.
agent_relevance: Use a worst-case score when we do not trust our priors over candidate programs.

source: Grunwald and Langford (2004/2007) Suboptimal behavior of Bayes and MDL in classification under misspecification
finding: Bayes and two-part MDL for classifiers can be inconsistent when the model is wrong. The error stays bounded away from the best achievable error at every sample size.
numbers: Gap between Bayes-MAP error and best error can approach 0.1609 (largest at best-error 1/5). Upper bound on Bayes classifier error is H(mu), the binary entropy of the best error.
quote: Bayesian methods for classification can be inconsistent under misspecification
limits: Applies to one recipe (prior on classifiers crossed with a prior on error rates) and two-part MDL. Not a refutation of Bayes with a well-specified model.
agent_relevance: Selecting among crude hypotheses with a naive likelihood can fail even with unlimited data. Bayes does not rescue a wrong hypothesis space.

source: Grunwald and van Ommen (2017) Inconsistency of Bayesian inference for misspecified linear models, and SafeBayes
finding: With a homoskedastic Gaussian model on heteroskedastic data, the Bayes posterior puts mass on ever higher dimensional models as n grows, giving bad squared-error predictions. SafeBayes lowers the learning rate (likelihood exponent) to repair this.
numbers: Posterior inconsistent in both model-averaging/selection and ridge settings. SafeBayes picks a small learning rate when the posterior is not cumulatively concentrated.
limits: Simulation study on synthetic data; several SafeBayes variants (R- and I-) differ; one variant was uncompetitive.
agent_relevance: Temper the evidence (learning rate below 1) when the hypothesis space may be wrong.

source: Blier and Ollivier (2018) The description length of deep learning models
finding: Prequential (online) coding of MNIST and CIFAR10 labels gives much shorter codes than variational or two-part codes, even counting model cost. Variational codes, built to minimise the bound, are poor.
numbers: MNIST: prequential 4.10 kbits (ratio 0.021, 99.5% test accuracy) vs variational 24.1 kbits (ratio 0.12, 95.5%). CIFAR10: prequential 45.3 kbits (ratio 0.27, 93.3%) vs variational 89.0 kbits (ratio 0.54, 61.6%). Float32 two-part code about 32 Mbits.
quote: simple incremental encoding methods yield excellent compression values on deep networks
limits: Image classification only. Compute for repeated training is not counted in the code length.
agent_relevance: Prequential code length is a practical selection score that includes learning cost.

source: Deletang et al. (2024) Language modeling is compression
finding: A prediction model plus arithmetic coding is a lossless compressor. Chinchilla 70B, trained mainly on text, compresses images and audio better than PNG and FLAC.
numbers: ImageNet patches 43.4% of raw size vs PNG 58.5%; LibriSpeech 16.4% vs FLAC 30.3%. Chinchilla 70B enwik9 raw rate 8.3% vs gzip 32.3% and LZMA2 23.0% (2048-byte chunks).
limits: Raw rate ignores model size. Counting parameters (two-part code, float16) removes the advantage of large models on 1GB of data.
agent_relevance: Code length is log loss. Counting model size is the MDL step usually skipped in LLM claims.

source: Deletang et al. (2024) adjusted versus raw compression
finding: Adjusted rate adds model bytes (two-part code). Large models suffer a huge loss in adjusted rate that 1GB of data cannot offset. Prequential accounting would help over-parametrised nets (Blier and Ollivier) but was not run because online training is costly.
numbers: Further compressing float16 weights of a 38M Transformer gave only 92.2% (gzip) and 89.1% (LZMA2). Random data rates are about 100% or above for all compressors.
limits: Offline setting only.
agent_relevance: If we use an LLM as a prior over hypotheses, its description cost must be stated.

source: Deletang et al. (2024) generative use of gzip
finding: Any compressor gives a conditional generative model. gzip image completions are much noisier than Chinchilla 70B completions.
numbers: Qualitative comparison on image continuation; Chinchilla error accumulates with sample length.
limits: Figure only, no scores.
agent_relevance: Prediction and compression are one object; a good code is a good predictor.

source: Elmoznino et al. (2025) In-context learning and Occam's razor
finding: Next-token loss summed over an in-context sequence equals prequential code length. Training ICL to minimise it rewards low training error and low model complexity together, which explains why ICL generalises.
numbers: Meta-dataset of 10000 tasks with 2000 points each (80/20 split); tasks include noisy regression, sinusoids, Mastermind, HMMs. Prequential ICL beat a learner trained on train error alone on held-out tasks.
limits: GPT-4 on Mastermind had worse prequential cross-entropy than a small trained ICL model and than a naive marginal baseline (5 seeds). A big pretrained LLM does not always compress a new task.
agent_relevance: Score each item before showing it, then sum: an MDL-style generalisation test. A big LLM is not automatically a good prior.

source: Elmoznino et al. (2025) Kolmogorov view versus Bayes view
finding: Authors argue the Kolmogorov (compression) view generalises the Bayes-optimal view of ICL and explains cases where ICL is not Bayes-optimal, such as Raventos et al 2024, where diverse pretraining yields a more uniform prior.
numbers: Von Oswald et al 2023: k-layer linear transformers can mimic k steps of gradient descent, a non-Bayesian learner.
limits: Theory plus small-scale experiments.
agent_relevance: Treat 'LLM as Bayesian' as a hypothesis, not a fact.

source: Elmoznino et al. (2025) prequential length bounds
finding: Prequential code length of data is at least about K(D); a learner compresses D well only when it generalises to that dataset.
numbers: Occam learner minimises K(p) - log2 p(D); prequential learner approximates it.
limits: Assumes tasks are generated by short programs.
agent_relevance: Run candidates item by item, scoring each before it is revealed (matches guardrail G3).

source: Voita and Titov (2020) Information-theoretic probing with MDL
finding: Probe quality is measured by online codelength (data plus model cost) instead of accuracy. Accuracy fails to separate real labels from random control tasks; codelength does.
numbers: Across 10 probe settings accuracy ranked real vs control wrongly in 8 of 10; MDL was always correct. MDL results stable across random seeds and probe settings; accuracy was not.
limits: ELMo layers and few linguistic tasks. Online code was easier and gave tighter bounds than the variational code.
agent_relevance: Select by code length including the cost of the fitting procedure, not by accuracy of a flexible probe.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Compression represents intelligence linearly
finding: Across 31 public LLMs and 12 benchmarks, average benchmark score is almost linear in compression of external text corpora.
numbers: Pearson about -0.95 per domain (knowledge and commonsense, coding, math); about -0.93 overall.
limits: Correlation across models, not a within-model causal test; needs corpora not seen in training.
agent_relevance: Log loss on fresh text is a cheap unsupervised signal of model quality.

source: Dziugaite and Roy (2017) Nonvacuous generalization bounds via PAC-Bayes
finding: First nonvacuous numerical bounds for SGD-trained networks with more parameters than data, by optimising a PAC-Bayes posterior. The KL term acts as a description length.
numbers: VC-style bounds are vacuous even with 72 hidden units on MNIST. Experiments use n=150000 and delta=0.01.
limits: Bound is for a stochastic network; random labels give bounds near 50% error.
agent_relevance: Prior-times-fit bounds can be tight enough to rank hypotheses; compression and Bayes meet in PAC-Bayes.

source: Lotfi et al. (2022) PAC-Bayes compression bounds so tight
finding: Quantising weights in a low-dimensional subspace gives tight bounds: large models compress a lot, which supports Occam as an explanation of generalisation.
numbers: MNIST LeNet5 best bound 11.55% (SGD), 11.20% (full batch) error; best earlier MNIST bound cut by 94% (6.23 KB to 0.38 KB); ImageNet by 87% (358 KB to 46.3 KB); CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 bound 74.68%.
limits: CIFAR-10 bounds are still loose. Subspace dimension matters; some settings give 100% error bounds.
agent_relevance: Short descriptions of trained models track generalisation, a basis for a simplicity prior.

source: Xie, Raghunathan, Liang, Ma (2022) In-context learning as implicit Bayesian inference
finding: If pretraining data comes from a mixture of HMMs with latent concepts, a Bayes-optimal predictor infers the shared concept in the prompt and ICL appears. Synthetic GINC data confirms it.
numbers: Accuracy rises with number of examples n and example length k; accuracy still improves from 81% to 85% going from 12 to 16 layers.
limits: Synthetic mixture of HMMs; real LLMs are not shown to be Bayes-optimal.
agent_relevance: A concrete Bayesian story for prompts: examples narrow a latent-concept posterior.

source: Grau-Moya et al. (2024) Learning universal predictors
finding: Training LSTMs and Transformers on data from random programs on universal Turing machines moves them toward Solomonoff induction. The Solomonoff prior weights each program by 2^-length: a Bayes prior that is also a code.
numbers: Solomonoff bound: for any computable source mu, summed squared prediction error times 1 is below K(mu) ln 2. Tests include 15 Chomsky-hierarchy tasks.
limits: Computable approximation (bounded program length and steps); full SI is incomputable. I did not extract the result tables.
agent_relevance: A short-program prior is the ideal selection prior; trained nets only approximate it.

source: Rathmanner and Hutter (2011) A philosophical treatise of universal induction
finding: Solomonoff induction is Bayes with a universal prior 2^-K. It joins Occam, Epicurus and Bayes. The paper discusses no free lunch, black ravens, incomputability and reference-machine choice.
numbers: Total expected prediction error is bounded by a constant of order K(mu) ln 2 for any computable source.
limits: Incomputable; depends on the choice of reference machine.
agent_relevance: Justifies a simplicity prior while showing its practical limits.

source: MacKay (2003) Information Theory, Inference and Learning Algorithms, ch 28
finding: Bayesian evidence automatically penalises complex models (Occam factor), the Bayes counterpart of a description-length penalty. -log2 evidence is a code length.
numbers: Not opened; cited from memory of the book.
limits: Evidence is sensitive to prior width.
agent_relevance: The ratio of posterior to prior width prices flexibility; usable as a cheap complexity cost.

source: Hinton and van Camp (1993) Keeping neural networks simple
finding: First use of MDL and bits-back coding for neural network weights; basis of variational Bayes for nets.
numbers: Not opened; cited in Blier and Ollivier.
limits: Blier and Ollivier find variational codes give poor compression bounds on deep nets.
agent_relevance: Warns that an elegant Bayes-MDL bound can be loose in practice.

source: Barron, Rissanen, Yu (1998) The minimum description length principle in coding and modeling
finding: Survey linking MDL, Bayes mixtures and NML; mixture and two-part codes have redundancy near (k/2) log n.
numbers: Not opened; known through Grunwald and Roos.
limits: Claims here are secondhand.
agent_relevance: Background for choosing which code to use.

source: Grunwald and Roos (2019) luckiness examples
finding: Generalised-Jeffreys Bayes and luckiness NML coincide for some choices. Lasso is an MDL estimator with luckiness exp(-lambda/2 * sum |theta_j|), which is not a normalised prior.
numbers: Sparsity: log of (n choose k) grows about linearly in k, so models with few non-zero coefficients are favoured.
quote: That does not mean that we necessarily believe that the `truth' is sparse
limits: Choice of v is still subjective; the paper justifies it by hope of good prediction, not belief in truth.
agent_relevance: Priors in selection can be framed as hopes for good prediction.

source: Grunwald and Roos (2019) misspecification and learning rate
finding: When the model is wrong, MDL machinery can still be used by varying the learning rate (generalised Bayes), as in SafeBayes.
numbers: Section 6.3 explores the learning rate for non-Gaussian noise, briefly.
limits: Brief discussion only.
agent_relevance: Tempering is a practical fix when the hypothesis space is crude.
